keyword: what happens if you file taxes late

verifications.claim: Filing taxes late usually results in a failure-to-file penalty of 5% of unpaid taxes per month up to 25%
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Failure-to-file penalty: 5% of your unpaid tax bill for each month, or part of a month, that your return is late, up to 25%" (R2); "The late filing penalty is 5% of the tax due each month (or part of a month) your return is late... maximum penalty is 25%" (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources directly state the failure-to-file penalty as 5% per month up to 25% when filing late and owing taxes.

verifications.claim: Filing taxes late usually results in a failure-to-pay penalty of 0.5% per month
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Failure-to-pay penalty: 0.5% to 1% of your unpaid balance each month, also up to 25%" (R2); "The late-payment penalty is 0.5% of the unpaid balance for each month" (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Sources consistently describe failure-to-pay penalty as 0.5% per month as a consequence when filing late and owing taxes.

verifications.claim: If you are owed a refund, there is no penalty
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "If you miss the tax-filing deadline and are due a tax refund this year, then there will be no penalty associated with filing late" (R1); "If you’re expecting a tax refund, there’s no penalty for late filing" (R7)
verifications.reasoning: All relevant sources explicitly state no late-filing penalty if owed a refund.

verifications.claim: If you are owed a refund, you have three years from the deadline to file and claim it
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "You have up to three years from the tax-filing deadline to file your return and receive your refund" (R1); "You have three years from the due date of your tax return to file and claim your refund" (R7)
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources directly confirm the three-year window to claim refunds.

verifications.claim: The penalty for not filing is 5% per month
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "The penalty for failing to file a tax return is 5% of the unpaid tax per month" (R1); "Failure-to-file penalty is 5% of your unpaid tax bill for each month" (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Directly matches standard failure-to-file penalty description across sources.

verifications.claim: The penalty for not paying is 0.5% per month
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Failure-to-pay penalty: 0.5% of the unpaid taxes for each month" (R5); "failure-to-pay penalty is 0.5% of the tax owed after the due date, for each month" (R10)
verifications.reasoning: Consistently described as 0.5% per month for failure-to-pay.

verifications.claim: If both penalties apply, the combined penalty is 5% each month
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "If both penalties apply in the same month, the combined total is capped at 5%" (R5); "the failure-to-file penalty is reduced so that you are not paying more than 5% in penalties each month" (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Sources explicitly state the combined rate is 5% per month when both apply.

verifications.claim: The IRS charges interest on underpayments at the federal short-term rate plus 3%
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "interest on underpayments of tax is... the federal short-term rate plus 3%" (R4); "The interest rate is... federal short-term rate plus 3%" (R5)
verifications.reasoning: Exact rate formula confirmed in multiple IRS-related and explanatory sources.

verifications.claim: The IRS may file a substitute return on your behalf
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "the IRS may use a substitute for return to estimate your tax liability" (R2); "If you fail to file, we may file a substitute return for you" (R8)
verifications.reasoning: Direct IRS policy stated in official and secondary sources.

verifications.claim: A substitute return often misses out on deductions and credits you are entitled to
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "SFRs... Don’t claim business deductions... Don’t claim personal deductions... Don’t claim credits" (R2); "This return might not give you credit for deductions and exemptions you may be entitled to receive" (R8)
verifications.reasoning: Sources explicitly note substitute returns disadvantage taxpayers by omitting deductions/credits.

verifications.claim: The penalty stops accruing once you file
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Filing stops the larger penalty [failure-to-file] from accumulating" (R5); "Filing past-due returns quickly can reduce penalties" (R1)
verifications.reasoning: Refers to failure-to-file penalty stopping upon filing; failure-to-pay continues, but context supports for the key filing penalty.

verifications.claim: You can file Form 4868 for an automatic extension until October 15
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "complete IRS Form 4868... until October 15" (R1); "E-file Form 4868, Application for Automatic Extension... up to an additional 6 months" (R9)
verifications.reasoning: IRS sources and others confirm Form 4868 provides automatic extension to October 15.

verifications.claim: Form 4868 does not extend the time to pay taxes owed
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "it does not give you more time to pay your taxes if payments are due" (R1); "An extension of time to file is not an extension of time to pay" (R9)
verifications.reasoning: Explicitly stated in multiple sources including official IRS topic.

verifications.claim: The IRS offers installment agreements to pay off your balance over time
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Pay it in installments. You’ll attach IRS Form 9465 to your tax return to request an installment agreement" (R1); "you can apply for a Long-term payment plan (installment agreement)" (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Numerous sources confirm IRS installment agreement options.
